Who keeps property records in Williamson County?

That job belongs to the Williamson County Clerk, whose Official Public Records hold deeds, liens, lien releases, plats, restrictions, trusts and similar instruments. The clerk also staffs the probate court, the commissioners court and local birth, marriage and death registration, but land recording is the part a home seller touches. Each deed, deed of trust release and lien notice tied to a Williamson County house lands in that file.

  • Land recording and vital records counter: 1848 Texas Trail, Georgetown, TX 78626.
  • Court filings: the Justice Center, 405 Martin Luther King St., Georgetown.
  • Phone: 512-943-1515. Mail: PO Box 647, Jarrell, TX 76537-0647.
  • Hours: the recording counter runs 8 a.m. to 4:30 on weekdays, and the court floor stays open half an hour longer.

Under Attorney General Opinion WW-607, clerk staff cannot search records on your behalf or offer legal advice. You search online yourself, or a title company does it for you.

Searching Williamson County property records

Start at the clerk's Search Records page, which offers the Official Public Records Search, a judicial records search and a lookup for military discharge records.

Type the owner name from your deed or tax bill, then read forward from that deed. You are hunting for anything recorded afterward: a deed of trust, a release of lien, an abstract of judgment, a notice of foreclosure sale or an affidavit. The usual reason a lien still shows against a house the owner believes is paid off is a release that never got recorded. Under Local Government Code 192.007, any action on a recorded instrument has to be made by recording another instrument in the same manner, so the lender must file that release in this same office.

A map viewer on the county site helps too. Value and ownership data sit at the Williamson Central Appraisal District, yet its roll can lag behind recorded deeds. To learn who holds title, rely on the clerk.

What a deed needs to be accepted

To be recorded, a deed needs the owner's signature and either an acknowledgment taken by a notary or other authorized officer, or an oath before two witnesses (Property Code 12.001(b)). Owners who live out of state still record a Georgetown house in Georgetown.

Bring a current photo ID along with the document and payment, a requirement tied to House Bill 1195 of the 88th Legislature.

The clerk accepts many instrument types: general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds, plus affidavits, leases, sale contracts and powers of attorney. Filing a flawed deed does not cure it. The record simply tells the public what the paper says.

Recording fees

Williamson County posts its own totals in a 2024 Recording Fees PDF on the Fees page, so confirm the exact figure with the clerk. State law sets this base.

Statutory recording charges for a Texas county clerk
ChargeAmount
First page$5.00
Each added page, part page or attachment$4.00
Each name over five indexed$0.25
Records management and preservationUp to $10
Records archiveUp to $10
Records technology and infrastructure$2.00

Leave the grantee's mailing address off a deed and another $25 may apply. Some commissioners courts waive real property recording fees for buyers in particular grant programs. Ask whether Williamson County does.

Guarding against a fraudulent deed or lien

The clerk offers Property Fraud Alert at no charge. Register a name and you get an email or call each time a new document is filed under it.

When a judgment lien or conveyance on your house looks fake, the District Clerk runs a four-step cleanup.

  • Petition the District Clerk.
  • File an Owner's Affidavit of Purported Conveyance.
  • A district judge reviews the filing and signs findings of fact and conclusions of law.
  • File a certified copy of the signed order with the Official Public Records, free of charge.

The process rests on Government Code 51.902 and 51.903, and the District Clerk can tell you about a temporary restraining order. See a lawyer before filing.

Foreclosure notices and sales

Foreclosure auctions take place on each month's first Tuesday, outside the Justice Center at 405 MLK Street in Georgetown.

Lenders have to give notice of sale at least three weeks ahead, post it at the courthouse door and file it with the clerk. A borrower handed a notice of default has 20 days from receipt to reinstate by paying what is past due.

Any notice recorded against your house is searchable at the clerk. A sale before the auction date is possible, with the lender paid out of the buyer's money. Get the servicer's payoff figure in writing.

Recording transfers after an owner dies

The right document depends on how the estate is settled.

  • Transfer on death deed: record an affidavit of death with the death certificate.
  • Administered estate: record the executor's or administrator's deed.
  • Muniment of title: record the court's order along with the will.
  • No court case: an affidavit of heirship, which is a sworn statement and one a buyer need not accept.

Probate staff in the clerk's office accept applications and small estate affidavits. Chapter 205 of the Estates Code limits those to estates with no will and at most $75,000 in assets beyond homestead and exempt property, and a court must approve.

Nobody at the county can add heirs to an old deed. The person taking title records the proving paper, then the sale deed follows.

Liens at closing

Sellers often fear a lien will block the sale. Usually it will not, since paying it off at closing clears it. A title company finds what was recorded, asks for the payoff and arranges the release, and it will chase a lender that never filed one.

  1. Run your own name through the county's public records search.
  2. Write down each deed of trust, judgment or lien that turns up.
  3. Request a payoff statement or release from every holder.
  4. Share the list with your title company before any contract is signed.

With a cash buyer there is no loan underwriting, so closing speed depends mainly on how quickly those releases come in.

Market background

Williamson County is home to an estimated 752,827 people, 23.6 percent more than in April 2020. About 66.4 percent of housing units are lived in by their owners. Median home value is $447,000 and median gross rent is $1,796. With 4,956 building permits issued in 2025, new construction competes with resale listings.

Fast growth means many houses sit under recent deeds and loans, so their records are quick to review. Rural parcels, inherited homes and any house with an unreleased lien need paperwork cleanup before closing.

Frequently asked questions

Does the Williamson County Clerk run searches for me?

No. Clerk staff do not search records for the public, under Attorney General Opinion WW-607. Use the online Official Public Records Search or ask a title company.

Is photo ID required at the recording counter?

Yes. Bring a current photo ID with the document and payment, a rule tied to House Bill 1195.

Where can I find the exact recording fee?

On the clerk's Fees page, which links the 2024 Recording Fees PDF. The statutory figures in the table above are only the base.

Can I sell my Williamson County house with a lien on it?

Often yes, since a lien can be paid at closing. A title company can find the recorded lien, request the payoff and arrange the release, even when the lender never recorded one.

Is the county clerk the same office as the tax office?

No. The tax assessor-collector and the Williamson Central Appraisal District are separate offices. The clerk records documents and keeps probate and commissioners court records.

Recording a deed or lien release in person

Real estate paperwork goes to the Real Property Department of the Harris County Clerk, which takes any instrument a statute allows or calls for. Walk in at 201 Caroline, 3rd Floor, Suite 320. Weekday hours run 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the department's number is (713) 274-8680.

Get there early. Security screens every visitor, Suite 320 locks its door right at 4:30 p.m., and a plain copy requires you to be inside by 4:00 p.m. Because the county has more than 3.3 million residents, the clerk can demand a photo ID of whoever files at the counter. Each filer presents a personal government-issued ID; borrowing a colleague's will not work.

An annex office will accept a release of lien too, but the clerk says it may spend five to seven business days in transit downtown. When a closing date is tight, skip the annex: file downtown or send it electronically.

Mailing or e-recording a document

Both routes exist, each with strings attached. Address a mailed original to Attn: Real Property Department, P.O. Box 1525, Houston, TX 77251-1525, since the postal service delivers only to that box. A tracked courier shipment instead goes to 201 Caroline, 4th Floor, Suite 460, on weekdays.

For a mailed filing, enclose a cashier's check, money order or approved firm or business check from a U.S. bank. The clerk turns down cash, personal checks, temporary checks, estate, trust and association checks, and any check that has mark-outs.

Electronic filing runs through an approved vendor; Corporation Service Company, eRecording Partners Network and Simplifile are examples. State law restricts e-filers to attorneys, banks, credit unions, title insurers and their agents, state agencies and municipal clerks. Queue a document before 2:00 p.m. central time and it is handled that same business day. A later submission rolls to the next day. Most homeowners simply ask their title company or lender to submit for them.

Recording fees

The schedule is brief. A short deed with five or fewer names to index lands near the low end.

Harris County Clerk real property fees

Records management and archive charges went up from $6.00 to $10.00. Condominium declarations cost $10.00 per taped sheet, plus $50 for every key map page attached. Call to verify the total before you cut a check.

What the clerk needs on a document

The clerk records originals and certified copies of court documents, nothing else. A photocopy bounces back, and every bounce eats days. Check each item below first.

  • The signature must be an original and must be notarized, except for an IRS release.
  • Names are printed under every signature, with the capacity of the signer and the entity named.
  • Legal descriptions appear where they apply, along with a printed return address.
  • Leave a margin of 1 to 2 inches across the top and left side for recording information.
  • A conveyance shows each grantee's address, or the filer pays the greater of $25 or twice the recording fee.
  • An abstract of judgment shows the plaintiff's mailing address.

An original will is not filed in the real property records. Take it to the Probate Department for safekeeping instead. After probate, the court's certified copy of the will can be recorded, or the will can ride along as an exhibit to an affidavit of heirship.

Getting copies and guarding against fraud

Anyone can order certified or plain copies of recorded documents through the clerk's eCommerce feature. The Public Records Department, 713-274-6390, answers questions about the ordering process.

A free Property Alert System from the clerk sends a notice each time a new real property document is filed in your name. Landlords, owners with heirs and anyone with a title worry should enroll before listing. A surprise filing costs less to untangle before a buyer's title company spots it.

Tax value and ownership data live with a separate office, the Harris Central Appraisal District at hcad.org. Title companies comb the clerk's files for liens, judgments and unsettled heirs, and the sale generally waits until each one is released or paid.

Which recorded papers decide how fast a sale can close?

Title examiners trace the chain of recorded papers. Trouble spots usually trace back to a death or a skipped mortgage payment.

  • Death of an owner: the paper you need varies. An administered estate yields an executor's or administrator's deed; a muniment of title pairs a court order with the will; and an affidavit of heirship fills in when neither fits.
  • A transfer on death deed counts only when it was recorded while the owner was alive. An affidavit of death and the death certificate get recorded afterward.
  • A foreclosure sale notice must be filed with the clerk and posted at the courthouse at least 21 days before the first-Tuesday auction, which the state sets between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.
  • A deed of trust is cleared by a recorded release of lien, which the clerk accepts downtown and at the annexes.

No one can amend an old deed to add heirs. The remedy is a fresh instrument on record. Begin that paperwork before you list, since an affidavit or court order may take longer than the sale.

Steps before you list a Harris County house

A short routine saves most closings from delay. First, search the clerk's records under every owner name on the deed and find each deed of trust and its release. Second, sign up for the Property Alert System so a surprise filing reaches you. Third, check with the appraisal district that the owner of record matches the person who will sign. Fourth, if anyone on the chain has died, begin the probate or affidavit work right away. Fifth, gather originals: a photocopy will not be recorded, and the signer's notarized signature is required.

A cash sale skips most of the buyer's lender paperwork, but the title company still records the deed and any lien releases with the clerk. So the same record cleanup applies whether the buyer pays cash or finances.

Harris County housing market

Harris County is the most populous county in Texas: 5,045,026 people in the July 2025 estimate, up from 4,731,145 at the 2020 census. It counted 2,012,848 housing units, and 30,909 building permits were issued in 2025. Owners live in 54.7 percent of homes. Median home value is $276,600 and median rent is $1,401.

A county this size produces a heavy volume of deeds of trust, liens and affidavits of heirship. That volume is one reason the clerk insists on clean originals, precise fees and approved e-recording vendors.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Harris County Clerk's real property office?

The in-person counter is at 201 Caroline, 3rd Floor, Suite 320, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone number is (713) 274-8680.

Does the clerk require a photo ID to file?

Yes, for in-person filing. Texas law lets a clerk in a county of 3.3 million or more require photo identification, and each person shows their own valid government-issued ID.

Can I record a copy of my deed?

No. The clerk takes original documents with original signatures, or certified copies of court documents. A photocopy of a deed is refused.

How much does it cost to record a deed?

The posted schedule is $5.00 for the first page, $4.00 for each added page and $0.25 for each name over five, plus a $10.00 archive fee and a $10.00 management fee. Check the clerk's page for the latest amounts.

How do I get alerts when someone files a document under my name?

Sign up for the clerk's free Property Alert System. It notifies you of any new real property document filed under your name.

Where Dallas County property records are kept

For land records in Dallas County, go to the Recording Division of the County Clerk. It works from the Records Building, 500 Elm Street, Suite 2100, Dallas, TX 75202, and holds the Official Public Records: deeds, mortgages, releases and more.

The office records roughly 400,000 documents a year: deeds, liens against a property, transfers between owners, probate papers that touch land, and the release of lien filed once a mortgage is paid off. Its purpose is to show the public who holds a financial interest in a parcel.

  • Phone: (214) 653-7099
  • Hours: weekdays, opening at 8:00 a.m. and closing at 4:30 p.m., with court-approved holidays off
  • Mail: Dallas County Clerk's Office, Recording Division, 500 Elm Street, STE 2100, Dallas, Texas 75202
  • Questions the FAQ page does not answer: recording@dallascounty.org

A seller will touch this office through the title company, since the title search and the filing of the new deed both run through these records. Start at the Recording Division page.

Searching and copying records

Begin with the clerk's Online Public Record Search, which returns non-certified images. Pay for a certified copy only if a lender, court or title company demands it. The free search and the certified service are two different things.

Certified electronic copies of Official Public Record documents are sold on the clerk's website around the clock. Each carries the clerk's digital signature and tamper-proof encryption, so a buyer's lender can accept it without a paper original. Counter and mail requests for real property copies run $1.00 a page, and a certified copy adds $5.00 for each document.

Plat copies are priced separately: $6.00 per page for the large 18 by 24 size and $1.00 per page for 8.5 by 11, with the same $5.00 certification fee per plat. The clerk holds only plats filed with that office, so a subdivision map recorded elsewhere will not be there.

Recorded deeds sometimes carry a Social Security number, driver's license number, date of birth or bank account number. Under House Bill 2061, that information may be eligible for redaction. The owner files a Redaction Request Form by mail or in person. Any other change to a recorded document needs a later filing, so ask a lawyer whether a correction document or a fresh deed is the right fix.

Recording charges

A standard document costs $25.00 on page one and $4.00 on each page after. Of the $25.00, $5.00 pays for recording, $10.00 for records preservation and $10.00 for archiving.

Selected Dallas County Clerk recording and copy fees
Filing or serviceFee
First page of a standard document$25.00
Each remaining page$4.00 per page
Notice of Sale (foreclosure)$2.00
State tax lien, public filing fee$25.00
Federal tax lien, real estate or personal property$30.00
Tax certificate$4.00
Plain copy, real property records$1.00 per page
Certification added to a copy$5.00 per document

Writing on the back of the last sheet is billed as a full $4.00 page, so a signature block that spills onto a reverse side costs the same as a new page. A few specialty documents have their own fees, and some filings, such as child support liens and military discharge papers, carry no filing fee.

Payment rules are strict. Acceptable payment is cash, money order, cashier's check or business check, payable to the Dallas County Clerk. It does not accept personal checks. Cards work only in person, with a 2.05 percent convenience fee on credit and pinless debit or $2.85 on pin debit. Include a self-addressed stamped envelope with mailed filings if you want the stamped copy back.

What the clerk requires before recording a deed

The deed has to be signed and properly acknowledged, and a photo ID is required for documents that convey property from one person to another. House Bill 1195 put that rule in place on July 1, 2023.

  • Acknowledgment. A notary, another authorized officer or two subscribing witnesses must attest to the signature.
  • Court-ordered papers. Anything that originates in a lawsuit has to arrive as a certified copy, authenticated by the court or its clerk.
  • Grantee address. Leave off the buyer's mailing address and a $25 charge may follow.
  • Notary on site. A notary sits on the fourth floor in the Treasurer's office from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. daily for $10, cash only.
  • Electronic filing. Local Government Code Sec. 195.003 limits e-recording to attorneys, banks and credit unions, federally approved lenders, state-regulated lenders, title insurers and agents, and state agencies.

An individual who is not on that list files on paper at the Elm Street counter or by mail, or lets the title company submit the deed electronically after closing.

Dallas County housing at a glance

Dallas County had an estimated 2,661,397 residents in July 2025, up 1.9 percent from the 2020 base, across 873.06 square miles and 1,099,775 housing units. The owner-occupied rate is 50.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, so roughly half of households rent. With a tenant in the house, the title company will want the lease.

The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $303,000. Median gross rent is $1,565. Builders pulled 12,691 permits in 2025. Median monthly owner costs run $2,166 with a mortgage and $793 without one. A house with no mortgage is simpler to transfer, because there is no lender payoff and no release of lien to track down.

Record problems that slow a sale

Unreleased liens, unfiled estate paperwork and tax debts cause most delays, and all of them show up in the clerk's records. A title company runs the search before closing and flags what it finds.

  • Old mortgages. A paid-off loan should have a recorded release of lien. If none was filed, the lender has to be contacted to issue one.
  • Tax liens. State and federal tax lien notices are filed with the clerk, and the clerk lists fixed fees for both and for their releases.
  • Foreclosure notices. Notices of sale are posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk, usually 21 or more days before the sale.
  • Estates without a clean chain. An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement filed with the clerk, but no buyer or lender has to accept it. Probate or a court order may be safer.
  • Hospital and child support liens. Both have to be cleared if they attach to the property.

If any of these turn up, ask the title company which instrument cures the problem and who files it.

Property taxes at closing

The county's claim for each year's tax begins January 1 and rests on whoever holds title that day. A November sale leaves that claim in place, so the closing statement has to say who pays it.

Statements arrive near October 1. February 1 is when a balance goes delinquent, adding six percent penalty and one percent interest, and the penalty climbs a point a month through July 1. Installments are open to owners over 65 or disabled. Before closing, call the Dallas County tax office for the balance and ask the appraisal district whether a homestead exemption is on file. A buyer may be able to claim an unused exemption for the remainder of the year.

Frequently asked questions

What is the first-page charge for a deed at the Dallas County Clerk?

The first page is $25.00 and every extra page is $4.00. Of the first-page fee, $5.00 is for recording and $10.00 each is for records preservation and archiving. Anything printed on a page's back is billed as a full page.

Can I pay Dallas County recording fees with a personal check?

No. The clerk accepts cash, money orders, cashier's checks and business checks payable to the Dallas County Clerk. Cards are taken only in person, with a 2.05 percent convenience fee on credit and pinless debit cards or $2.85 on pin debit.

Are the documents in the online public record search certified?

No. Online search results are non-certified. Electronic certified copies carry the clerk's digital signature and are sold through a separate service. Paper certified copies are $1.00 a page plus $5.00 a document.

Can I e-record my own deed in Dallas County?

Usually not. Electronic recording is limited to attorneys, banks, certain lenders, title companies and state agencies. An individual owner normally files on paper at 500 Elm Street or has a title company file the deed.

How do I remove a Social Security number from a recorded document?

File a Redaction Request Form with the clerk, by mail or in person. House Bill 2061 makes personal data such as Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, dates of birth and account numbers eligible for redaction.

A Southside Annex inside Precinct 1 at 3505 Pleasanton Rd. also takes filings, at 210-335-3522.

Doors open at 8 a.m. on weekdays and close at 5 p.m., with a later 5:45 closing on Wednesdays. The Deed Records desk, which pulls copies and researches liens, is in Suite B109 of the same tower at 210-335-2273. Mail goes to the Clerk's Office, Attn: Recordings, 100 Dolorosa, Suite 104, San Antonio.

Each month a "Records on the Run" satellite office moves between precinct offices and community centers, which can save a downtown trip. The clerk also runs a Vanguard Property Alert that warns owners about potentially fraudulent filings, and accepts wills for safekeeping.

Fees for filing a deed

A single page costs $25.00 to record, and each extra page adds $4.00. The first-page charge breaks into a $5.00 recording fee, a $10.00 records archive fee and a $10.00 records management fee, all effective January 1, 2024.

The clerk's fee page lists every total from 1 through 50 pages. Add-ons you are most likely to meet:

  • Notice of trustee sale: $2.00 filing, $1.00 for a plain copy
  • Federal tax lien instruments: $30.00 total

Filing rules

Bring originals bearing original signatures; copies are refused. Staff cashier each document, assign an instrument number and scan it while you wait, then hand back or return the original. Accepted payment is cash, credit card, check or money order, with checks made out to the Bexar County Clerk.

E-filing is its own lane. Local Government Code section 195.003 reserves it for attorneys, banks and credit unions, federally backed mortgage lenders, persons approved to make regulated loans, title companies, state agencies and municipal clerks. The clerk approves six providers, including CSC, Simplifile, ePN, Indecomm and Hopdox.

Staff will not draft a deed or vouch for clear title, and they refer anyone wanting assurance to a title company or attorney. Property Code 12.001(b) also requires a conveyance to be signed and acknowledged before a notary or similar officer before it is recorded.

Checking for liens before you sell

Try the clerk's public records search first, or stop at the Deed Records Department, Suite B109 of the Paul Elizondo Tower, where staff can direct you to recorded liens on a property. The clerk does not guarantee clear title and takes no responsibility for encumbrances, so a guaranteed search comes from a title company, with an attorney as the other route.

Mortgage foreclosure notices can be pulled from the same search. A list is also available through the clerk's GIS Foreclosure Map or at the Deed Records counter. For the tax foreclosure list, call the law firm that handles those cases at 210-225-4422.

  • Release of lien: record the original in person at the tower or mail it to the courthouse office, at $25.00 for the first page
  • Lost deed: a certified copy runs $1.00 per page plus $5.00 per certification
  • Plain copies: found online under Land Records in the Official Public Records Search

For a seller, the practical order is simple. Search the records for your name and address, request payoff letters for any lien that appears, and ask for a tax certificate. Bring the payoff letters to the title company so each item can be released at closing. If a release was never recorded after an old loan was paid, the lender can record one, and the clerk's index will show it once it is filed. Resolve this before an offer, so the closing date is not at risk.

Run this check before listing, since a lien you did not know about can stall a contract. Cash buyers want clean title too, so the same search applies to a quick cash sale.

Foreclosure sales

Public cash auctions for mortgage and tax foreclosures take place on the first Tuesday of every month, 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. When that Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4, the sale moves to Wednesday. Bidding happens outdoors beside the courthouse, in the gap between it and the Paul Elizondo Tower, unless Commissioners Court names a different spot.

Bidders need no registration for a mortgage foreclosure, but registration is required to bid on a tax foreclosure. Only cash or certified funds work, and personal checks are refused. A GIS Foreclosure Map tracks notices and is refreshed twice a month, on the first Friday after the auction and about 18 days before the next sale.

An owner can buy back agricultural or homestead property within two years, and other property within six months, with the clock running from the day the sale deed is recorded. A free foreclosure training seminar meets on each first Tuesday. Notice of a sale has to be posted and filed with the clerk 21 or more days before it.

Market context for sellers

Bexar County had an estimated 2,160,088 residents in mid-2025, 7.5 percent above the 2020 base, in 853,619 housing units. Owners live in 58.8 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $262,200, and typical monthly rent is $1,354.

Values and tax collection

Two offices split the tax work: the Bexar Central Appraisal District handles valuation and protests, and the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector takes payments. BCAD takes no tax payments. It mails value notices to new owners and to anyone whose market value climbed $1,000 or more, and a protest can be filed without a notice.

For tax certificates and payment questions, call 210-335-6628, at the Vista Verde Plaza Building. Across Texas, value is fixed each January 1, bills arrive in October, and unpaid tax turns delinquent February 1. School districts exempt $140,000 of a homestead, and seniors or disabled owners receive $60,000 on top.

Mind the lien. Each January 1 the year's tax lien attaches to the land, so a closing agent will ask for a current tax certificate and proof that earlier years are paid. Order the certificate early in the sale so a surprise balance does not delay closing.

Frequently asked questions

What is the first-page fee for a deed?

The total is $25.00, built from a $5.00 recording fee and two $10.00 charges, one for the archive and one for records management. Pages after the first cost $4.00 each.

Will the clerk record a photocopy of my deed?

No. Only the signed original is accepted. Take it to the Paul Elizondo Tower or mail it to the courthouse office.

Which day are foreclosure auctions held?

Monthly, on the first Tuesday, with bidding from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. A first Tuesday that lands on January 1 or July 4 pushes the sale to Wednesday.

Can I order a certified deed copy by mail?

Yes. Write to the clerk's courthouse office, or ask at the Deed Records Department inside the Paul Elizondo Tower. Expect $1.00 a page plus $5.00 for certification.

Does the appraisal district collect property tax?

No. Its work is values, exemptions and protests. For payments and tax certificates, call the Bexar County Tax Assessor-Collector at 210-335-6628.

Where to record a deed in Tarrant County

Land records go to Records Intake in Room B20 of the historic Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. Land-related documents can be recorded only there, not at the sub-courthouses.

Filing works three ways: in person from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, by post with the original plus a check or money order made out to the Tarrant County Clerk, or through the county's eRecording process. Walk-in filers must show a driver's license or ID, while mailed documents do not need a copy of one.

Staff will not notarize, advise you on the law or fill in forms for you. Get the deed notarized ahead of time. Intake takes only originals or clerk-certified copies.

Recording fees

On most documents the first page costs $20 and every page after it $4. A notice of trustee sale runs $10. Printing on both sides of a sheet counts as two pages.

The counter takes cash, cards, checks and money orders, and cards add a small convenience fee. Some document types follow different fee rules, so confirm yours with the clerk.

Searching Tarrant County property records

The County Clerk Official Records Search is free to browse. Once you find a document, register for an account and download an unofficial watermarked copy at no charge. That is enough for your own research.

If a lender or title company wants a certified copy, you can buy one through the same system. Choose the certified-copy icon, pay the calculated fee, then pick up the file under Order History in your account. Certified copies are also sold in person at Room B30 of the courthouse, or by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope and the document number.

New filings do not appear instantly. Expect a recorded document to turn up on the search site 5 to 7 business days later. Intake scans and indexes it while you wait and hands you an instrument number, which is your proof of filing in the meantime. Title searches, lien searches and restriction reviews are not done by clerk staff. A title company handles them.

What the clerk will and will not record

Records Intake takes documents that the law allows to be recorded, chiefly those that concern land: deeds, deeds of trust, liens and releases, some land affidavits, and plats.

Four kinds of documents get turned away:

  • Documents with no statutory authority behind their filing.
  • Documents that are not regular on their face.
  • Documents not properly signed in front of an officer such as a notary.
  • Copies that are neither originals nor clerk-certified.

Wills get special treatment. Intake records only probated wills, and a person who wants a will kept at the courthouse can leave it with the Probate office in Room B90 for a $5 fee. A conveyance must be signed and acknowledged, or sworn before two witnesses, under Texas law before it is recorded. Common deed types include general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds.

Why recorded documents matter when you sell

Before closing, the buyer's title company reads every recorded document on your parcel, and anything left unreleased can hold up the sale. Common trouble spots are an old deed of trust never released, a lien, an affidavit that clouds title, and a missing deed on an inherited property.

A tax lien exists without any recording. It attaches every January 1, and clear title is impossible for a buyer until delinquent taxes are paid. Liens filed by the state comptroller are recorded with the county clerk, so you may see them in the clerk's records.

Once a lender begins foreclosure, a notice of trustee sale shows up in the clerk's records. Foreclosure sales in Texas are auctions, and for unpaid taxes a constable or an agent hired by the taxing unit runs the sale. Seeing that notice on your house still leaves choices: repay the debt, list the house, or accept a cash offer that closes ahead of the sale date.

Probate and the rest of the clerk's work

The county clerk serves as recorder, as clerk of the commissioners court, and as the office receiving probate filings like applications and small estate affidavits. In Tarrant County the real property side and the probate side sit in different rooms of the same courthouse, with probate in Room B90.

If the house came to you after someone died, the split affects your timing. Heirs may need probate papers filed before anyone can sign a deed, and those go through a different line than the deed. Plan a separate trip or mailing for each, and ask the title company what must be recorded first.

Title companies and escrow agents also have account options. An OPR Escrow Payments route exists for the Official Public Records, with 817-884-1062 for completing the process after an online payment, and a separate bulk data payment route at 817-884-1069. Most individual sellers never need either, but your title company might use the first.

Property fraud alerts

Tarrant County offers a Property Fraud Alert sign-up, linked from its Real Estate Records page. Use that link to see how alerts work and what they cover.

A yearly check or two of your own name and address in the Official Records Search is a smart habit. Watch for any deed or lien you cannot explain, and if one appears, carry its instrument number to the clerk and to a title company.

Recording is public by design. That helps buyers and lenders trust the chain of title, but it also means anyone can see what was filed against your parcel, and a forged deed that gets recorded still has to be unwound through the courts.

Preparing your papers for a sale

Whether you plan to list or accept a cash offer, start by downloading your recorded deed from the Official Records Search and reading it. Check that every owner name is spelled correctly and that the legal description matches your tax bill. Errors found now are far cheaper to fix than errors found at the closing table.

  1. Search your name and address for any deed of trust and confirm it was released after payoff.
  2. Look for liens, judgments or affidavits filed against the parcel.
  3. If the house was inherited, confirm the probate papers and the deed into your name were filed.
  4. Order a certified copy of anything the title company asks for.
  5. Get the deed notarized before you go to Room B20, or mail it with the right fee.

A cash buyer still needs a title company to examine these records, but the lack of a lender's underwriting means fewer parties waiting on paperwork.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Tarrant County?

Most documents cost $20 for the first page and $4 for each added page. A document printed on both sides counts as two pages.

Where is the Tarrant County Clerk's records office?

Records Intake is in Room B20 of the Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. It is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Can I record a deed by mail in Tarrant County?

Yes. Mail the original to Room B20 with a check or money order payable to the Tarrant County Clerk, and work out the fee from the page count. The deed must already be notarized.

Can I get a copy of my deed for free?

Yes, an unofficial watermarked copy downloads free from the Official Records Search after you register for an account. Certified copies cost $1 per page plus $5 for certification.

How long before a recorded deed shows online in Tarrant County?

Generally 5 to 7 business days after recording. Walk-in filers get an instrument number while they wait.

Where to record and find records in Travis County

The Guadalupe Street location takes Official Public Record recording, DBA filings and marriage licenses with no appointment, but not plat recording. The main recording phone line is (512) 854-9188.

The Travis County market in brief

Travis County includes Austin and has grown quickly. Population was 1,389,670 in mid 2025, up from 1,290,188 at the 2020 Census. Typical owner-occupied home value is $523,000, 52.1 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and median gross rent is $1,744.

That mix means deed work here includes many investor sales, estate transfers and rental properties. Volume also keeps the recording desk busy, since deeds, releases of lien, trustee sale notices and plats all flow through the same division. Filing early in the day and using a title company's e-filing channel avoids most delays at the counter.

How filing works

Bring or mail the original signed document, because the clerk will not record a copy. Real property documents can be filed in person or by mail, and recording is complete as soon as the clerk receives the document.

Most documents other than plats are scanned, given an instrument number and returned the same day, by mail or immediately for walk-in customers. Subdivision plats are not returned the same day. Pay with cash, credit card, check or money order payable to Travis County Clerk. Card payments add a fee: $3 on transactions under $100 or 3 percent on $100 or more.

A deed must also meet the state's execution rule: it must be acknowledged before a notary or other officer, or sworn before two subscribing witnesses, under Property Code Section 12.001(b).

Searching records online

The clerk's public records search is at tccsearch.org. Indexes for most recorded documents are online, and redacted images of recordings run from the mid 1980s to the present. Redacted images have personal identifiers such as Social Security numbers blocked.

Court case data updates every 24 hours, and newly filed document images take about 72 hours to appear online. The permanent library holds millions of older documents dating to the 1800s, with older ones on microfilm.

Who can file electronically

eRecording is limited to specific filers under Local Government Code Section 195.003, including Texas attorneys, banks and credit unions, title insurance companies and agents, federally approved lenders, regulated lenders and state agencies.

Anyone interested in becoming an approved submitter can contact the clerk's office. A homeowner selling alone does not qualify directly, so most sellers go through a title company, which typically e-files the deed on closing day.

Liens, trustee sales and taxes

Expect the record to show more than the deed. Liens, trustee sale notices and tax liens are filed with the same clerk. A notice of trustee sale of real estate is posted for a $2.00 fee, and state and federal tax liens have their own filing charges.

Property tax is a separate system: the appraisal district sets value and local taxing units bill, while the clerk only records documents. For closing figures, ask the Travis County tax office for the current bill. Before listing, search the owner's name for open liens and make sure the deed in your chain matches the name on the contract.

Certified copies and older records

A certified copy is made by a clerk, who stamps it as an accurate and complete reproduction of the original. Certification costs $5.00 per document plus $1.00 per page, and you can request one by phone, email or in person.

No recording sticker goes on the last page of a certified copy, so one extra $4.00 page is always added. Copies of federal documents cost $1.50 per page and state documents $1.00 per page, and an 18 by 24 inch plat copy is $3.00 per page. If you need a certified copy of a vesting deed for a sale, ask early, because a lender or title company usually wants the recorded instrument number as well.

Most fees cannot be refunded, though clerical errors may qualify, and a service already performed is generally not refundable.

Getting ready to sell

A tidy record helps any sale, and it matters most when a buyer is paying cash and wants to close quickly. Here is a short order of work:

  1. Search your own name online and read the deed that put you on title.
  2. Look for any deed of trust that was paid off but never released, and any lien or trustee sale notice.
  3. Ask the tax office for the current bill and any balance.
  4. If you need a certified copy, request it early and note the instrument number.
  5. Choose a title company, which will e-file the deed and handle the fees on closing day.

With the record clean, a cash sale can close in a short time, since there is no lender waiting on appraisal and underwriting. If the record shows a problem, you will at least know about it before the buyer does.

No. The clerk requires the original document with original signatures. Plan on a notarized original when you file.

Paper filings arrive by mail or at the counter. Electronic filings must go through an approved partner, and you choose a partner before submitting. Each partner can explain its own process.

Denton County housing at a glance

Denton County is growing quickly, and its housing is newer and pricier than most of Texas. The July 2025 estimate is 1,069,346 residents, an 18.0 percent rise on the 2020 count of 906,530 and well above the 662,614 counted in 2010. Land area is 878.51 square miles, and density was 1,031.8 residents per square mile in 2020.

  • Housing units: 415,326 in 2025, with 10,210 building permits that year
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 65.5 percent for 2020 to 2024
  • Middle owner-occupied home value: $437,200
  • Median gross rent: $1,728

With that much new building, new construction competes with resale listings all over the county, and many sellers own homes in recorded subdivisions. The plat matters. The clerk files plats at $50 per page, and a copy of a plat on file is $5. A buyer's title company will want the plat and any other recorded restrictions.

What to check in the records before listing

Pull the vesting deed, the deed of trust and any releases, then compare the names and legal description against the tax records. Mismatches are easy to fix before an offer and slow to fix after one.

  • Name and legal description. The seller's name on the deed should match the name on the sale contract, and the lot and block should match the plat.
  • Liens. A state tax lien, federal tax lien or unreleased mortgage will be visible in the clerk's index, and the schedule lists a fee for each filing and for the federal release.
  • Foreclosure posting. The county posts notice of a trustee's sale and charges the clerk's $2 notice fee. Texas sales take place on the first Tuesday of the month.
  • Heirs. For an inherited house, a death-transfer deed has to be on record before the owner dies, and a muniment of title goes to the clerk in the land's home county.

If anything on the list looks off, ask the title officer how the problem gets cleared. Some defects need only a release. Others need a corrective deed or a court order.

How property tax hits a Denton County seller

The tax lien attaches on January 1, so the bill for the year follows the property no matter when the sale closes. Appraisal districts set value as of that date, and tax bills usually go out in October.

The last day to pay without penalty is January 31, and February 1 starts delinquency. The collector then adds a six percent penalty and one percent interest, with the penalty rising to 12 percent on July 1. Homeowners age 65 or older, disabled owners and disabled-veteran owners can pay in four installments.

Texas has no state property tax, so the whole bill comes from local units such as the county, school district and city. Ask the Denton County tax office for the current balance before closing, and ask the appraisal district to confirm any homestead, over-65 or disabled-veteran exemption on file. A school district must give a $140,000 homestead exemption.

Selling with a recording problem

Most delays come from paperwork, not price. If the deed has a typo in a name, if a paid-off loan never got a release, or if the owner has died and no one has filed the estate, the closing slips. Start with a list: the vesting deed, each loan, and any lien notice. Hand the list to the title officer on day one.

When a document has to be corrected, the fix is a new recorded instrument. Because every filing must go to the Denton location, build in mailing time or choose an e-recording partner. Allow for the $25 first page plus the required $4 information page when you budget the filing cost.

Frequently asked questions

Which office files a Denton County deed?

The County Clerk's Recording Division, 1450 E. McKinney Street in Denton. You can also mail it to that address or file electronically through a clerk-approved partner. All recordings must go to the Denton location, not to the other clerk offices.

What are the Denton County Clerk's hours?

The Recording Division serves the public on weekdays from 8 in the morning to half past four at 1450 E McKinney Street. Recordings go to that Denton office only.

What does a deed filing cost in Denton County?

$25 for the first page, $4 for a required recording information page and $4 for each additional page, with printing on the back counted as a page. The first-page charge includes $10 for records preservation and $10 for archiving.

What forms of payment does the Denton County recording office accept?

Business checks, cash, cashier's checks, credit cards and money orders. Mail-in filings paid by card need the clerk's Credit Card Payment Form, and mailed filings need the matching request and payment form.

Can I record a document electronically in Denton County?

Yes, but only through one of the clerk's electronic recording partners. Choose a partner first, and it will explain its own steps.

The Hidalgo County Clerk's recording role

Under the state constitution the county clerk serves as "Recorder of the County." In Hidalgo County that job sits with the Recording Department, which handles four tasks for every instrument: deciding whether to accept it, filing it, recording it and indexing it. The clerk's website lets you search, view, print and download land records.

The department takes warranty deeds, trustee's deeds, state and federal tax liens, foreclosures, judgments, subdivision plats and financing statements. Assumed name certificates go through the same department. Beyond recording, the clerk's office holds court records, vital records, marriage licenses and probate files, which makes a single visit useful for an estate sale.

Before you travel with a filing, phone the clerk and ask which counter or online route fits it.

Searching official records online

The clerk's Official Records Search leads to the county portal at hidalgo.tx.publicsearch.us. Working from a checklist saves time. Before listing the house or signing a contract, pull each of these:

  • The vesting deed that placed the current owner on title.
  • All deeds of trust, with a recorded release for any loan that was repaid.
  • Tax liens, judgments and foreclosure postings under the owner's name.
  • Any plat or subdivision record that touches lot lines or easements.

Try every spelling variation of each owner's name, including hyphenated and compound surnames and middle names. One missed spelling can hide an old lien until a title company finds it. Search again shortly before closing, because new items can be filed after your first look.

Filing fees for a deed

Recording a deed into the Official Public Records costs a flat opening charge plus a small amount for each added page.

Hidalgo County Clerk deed recording charges

Senate Bill 1612 repealed a $1.00 document filing fee, and the clerk dropped it from official public records recordings, assumed names, foreclosure notice postings, plats and marriage licenses. The posted schedule carries a 2024 title, so call the clerk to confirm the current figure before you send payment.

Across Texas, recording charges are assembled from per-page amounts plus records management, archive and technology pieces, and $25 more where a grantee mailing address is missing. Each county blends them its own way, so only Hidalgo's posted schedule applies to a Hidalgo filing.

The signer must first acknowledge the deed to a notary or comparable officer, or swear to it with two witnesses present (Property Code 12.001(b)). Recording happens in the county where the land lies.

Why records matter in the Hidalgo County housing market

Hidalgo County counts 921,549 residents and 329,360 housing units, with 67.5% of homes owner-occupied. A middle-valued owned home is worth $140,900, with middle gross rent at $957 and middle household income at $54,338. Households average 3.27 people. With values in that range, even a modest lien can eat a big share of a seller's equity.

For many local families the house is the biggest asset they own. Unpaid tax, or a deed that only one relative signed, can freeze a sale. When a property moves down through relatives with no probate case, the record chain has a hole that the buyer's title company will want filled.

Who values and taxes a Hidalgo County house?

The Hidalgo County Appraisal District, created January 1, 1980, appraises property and administers exemptions for the county's taxing units. An eight-member board appointed by those units runs it, and the county assessor-collector holds a voting seat. Cities, school districts, utility districts and the county each set their own rate, and the district's values feed every one of them.

The state sets the valuation date at January 1, the same date the year's tax lien takes hold. Expect bills near October 1. Anything unpaid by the end of January is delinquent from February 1, at which point a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest are added. If you think the value is wrong, a protest is normally due in mid-May.

Online, the district's portal shows valuations and tax data and accepts appeals and exemption applications. Homestead owners can claim $140,000 off school district value; seniors and disabled owners take $60,000 more off school tax. After a homestead exemption begins, the appraised value cannot grow by more than 10 percent annually.

Record issues that come up in Hidalgo County sales

Heirs, contract for deed sales, old liens and unpaid tax cause most delays. Each leaves a paper trail with the clerk, and each costs less to repair before a buyer's title company raises it.

  • Heirs with no probate case. Probate of a will is available for four years after death, and a muniment of title order lets the will pass title without an administration. For estates worth $75,000 or less, not counting the homestead and exempt property, a small estate affidavit may do the job.
  • Contract for deed. When a seller keeps title under a residential contract, Property Code chapter 5, subchapter D requires a yearly January statement to the buyer and gives the buyer cancellation rights within set periods.
  • Unreleased deeds of trust. A repaid loan with no recorded release still clouds title.
  • Delinquent tax. Four installments are open to seniors and disabled owners, and a few collectors offer homestead payment plans as long as 36 months.

Several of these fixes take weeks. Ask the lender for a release, file the probate matter through the clerk's probate staff, and pay any tax balance to the collector. Put whichever item the title company says blocks closing at the front of the line.

What to do if you are unsure which record is the problem

Request confirmation from the Recording Department of everything indexed under the owner's name, and carry the results to a title company along with the vesting deed, your latest tax statement and the names of all past owners. From those papers a title officer can usually spot the gap, lien or missing signature in your way.

After that the steps are simple. Collect lender releases, file the probate or affidavit paperwork that fits, pay the collector, and ask the title company to verify that each item was recorded. A cash buyer taking the house as-is skips a lender's appraisal and repair demands, yet every recorded item must still be cleared before money changes hands. Allow extra weeks if a probate filing is involved, and tell the buyer early so the closing date reflects it.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I find a Hidalgo County deed?

Search the clerk's official records portal at hidalgo.tx.publicsearch.us, or ask the Recording Department. Land records can be searched, viewed, printed and downloaded online.

What does it cost to file a deed in Hidalgo County?

The clerk's fee page lists $35 for the opening page and $4 for each page after it, on a schedule titled 2024. Verify the present amount with the office before filing.

Is the appraisal district the same as the county clerk?

No. The appraisal district sets values and administers exemptions, while the clerk records deeds and liens. A recorded deed does not by itself change a homestead exemption.

Can heirs sell a Hidalgo County house without probate?

Sometimes. A transfer on death deed recorded before the owner died, or a small estate affidavit for an estate of $75,000 or less (homestead and exempt property excluded), can move title without full administration. The buyer's title company decides whether to accept the paperwork.

What does a contract for deed change about my record?

The seller keeps title until the buyer pays in full, so the recorded deed still shows the seller. The annual January statement and the buyer's right to cancel come from Property Code chapter 5, subchapter D.

Older deeds and the Waxahachie courthouse

Texas carved the county out of Navarro County on December 20, 1849, and the seat was named Waxahachie. Records here run back a long way, and the present courthouse, accepted in 1897, is the fourth on the site. Earlier buildings included an 1850 log cabin, a frame building in 1854 and a limestone courthouse around 1870.

Recording needs a signature plus a notary-style acknowledgment or two witnesses. After a death the clerk cannot amend the earlier deed to list heirs. A new instrument must carry them.

Ellis County is served by Avalon, Ennis, Ferris, Italy, Maypearl, Midlothian, Milford, Palmer, Red Oak and Waxahachie school districts. The district a house sits in affects the school tax portion of the bill.

Preparing to record an Ellis County sale

Bring a check made out to the Ellis County Clerk, and add the extra $4.00 for each page after the first. If the deed runs onto a second page with only a signature block, you still pay for it. A cash sale skips the lender paperwork, which leaves fewer instruments to record. The deed, any prior lien release and the tax payoff are usually the whole list.

Homestead protections when selling

Buyers closing in spring or summer should ask the appraisal district about claiming a homestead right away, because an exemption can start mid-year when the seller never held one. Rockwall County Clerk's property records office

Deeds, deeds of trust, lien filings and plats for Rockwall County go through the Clerk's Property Department at Suite 100, 1111 E Yellowjacket Lane, Rockwall, TX 75087. Most GPS and internet maps put the building in the wrong spot. It sits about 0.3 miles east of Goliad and SH 205.

  • Open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m., closed on county holidays.
  • Cutoff: final transactions should be finished by 4 p.m.
  • ID: since House Bill 1195, a valid ID is required for any document presented in person.

The Official Public Records can be searched online, and copies and eCertified copies can be bought there. Paper certified copies are mailed by the clerk's office. A buyer who picks the In Person option can fill a cart online but pays at the counter.

Treat the online search as a starting point. House Bill 4350, effective June 20, 2025, requires some information to be redacted from certain instruments, so a screen may show a record that is incomplete or altered. Title examiners work from the official records at the clerk's office.

Filing fees

Plan on $25 for page one and $4 for each page after it. Senate Bill 1612 repealed the old $1 filing fee under Local Government Code Section 291.008(d) from January 1, 2024.

Document or serviceFee
First page of a document$25
Each additional page$4

Plats also need tax certificates, which are filed at their regular price. The clerk cannot refund an overpayment made by check, so call the office to confirm what applies to your instrument before you send it.

Formatting rules that get filings rejected

Paperwork gets turned away over format more often than you would expect. The county's general requirements include:

  • Leave a 2-inch by 4-inch area empty at the foot of the final page for the certification label. If the area is crowded the label goes on the back, which adds a page and a $4 charge. E-filed documents follow the same rule.
  • Signatures must be originals or certified copies, since the clerk cannot file copies.
  • Print or type each name below its signature line.
  • An abstract of judgment that omits the plaintiff's address costs double to file.
  • A correction instrument has to conform to Texas Property Code Chapter 5.

Plats face a longer checklist. Sheet size runs from 18 by 24 inches up to 24 by 36. The clerk wants a single black-line copy with the original seals and signatures, a full legal description, notarized signatures and a surveyor's certification. Inside a city's extraterritorial jurisdiction the city must approve it. Original tax certificates from every taxing unit, dated within 90 days of filing and showing no delinquent tax, must come with it.

What must a deed show before the clerk accepts it?

Under Property Code Section 12.001(b), the clerk can record a real property conveyance only when it carries a signature plus an acknowledgment or sworn statement before a notary or similar officer, or two subscribing witnesses. County clerks serve as recorders, and filing happens in the county where the land is located.

Estate paperwork lands here too. For a muniment of title, the court order and will are lodged with the clerk in the property's county. A transfer on death deed has to be on record before the owner's death. The small estate affidavit suits an intestate estate worth $75,000 or less excluding the homestead, and a homestead copy is recorded with the clerk. An affidavit of heirship is only a sworn statement that no court has checked, and nothing obliges a buyer or lender to rely on it.

A seller with a gap in the title should pull the chain of records early. A missing heir, an unreleased lien or an unrecorded deed will surface at the title company, and the cure usually means a fresh filing in this office.

Foreclosure notices and mechanic's lien bonds

Foreclosure notices are posted on the county's site. Trustee sales happen on the first Tuesday of each month outside on the courthouse steps at 1111 Yellowjacket Lane. The notice of sale is filed with the clerk and posted at the courthouse door at least 21 days beforehand, and the auction takes place between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. After a notice of default, the borrower has 20 days to reinstate by paying what is past due.

Mechanic's liens have an exit in this office. Under Property Code Sections 53.171 to 53.174, anyone may file a bond to indemnify against a lien. The lien is discharged once a compliant bond is filed, notice goes to each claimant by certified mail, and the bond and notice are recorded. The bond must generally be double the lien amount, or when the claims top $40,000, the larger of 1.5 times the liens or $40,000 plus the liens. The clerk charges the usual $25 and $4 page fees, plus $1 a page for copies and the mailing postage.

A free service called Property Fraud Alert sends a phone or email warning when a document is recorded under your name. One phone number can enroll 3 names and one email address can enroll 4.

Who handles Rockwall County values and tax bills?

On the first Tuesday of every month, at the front steps of the Rockwall County Courthouse. Questions go to the trustee named on a notice.

The clerk's website hosts a searchable real property database. Use it at home or on the public computers in the Angleton office. New users create a login and answer a verification email before searching. Clerks are recorders rather than qualified examiners, so a title search is not something they do for you. Recording fees

One page of deed costs $25.00 to record: $10.00 for records management, $10.00 for the records archive and $5.00 for the first page. Every additional page adds $4.00. Names indexed beyond the first five add $0.25 each.

Formatting rules

A long checklist comes from the clerk, and missing one line can get a deed rejected. Since January 1, 2026, anyone presenting a real property document in person must show photo ID to the clerk, under Local Government Code 191.010.

An inherited house needs more proof. Filing an affidavit of heirship with the county clerk records a sworn statement that no court has verified, and nothing requires a buyer or lender to accept it. An order from the probate court, or a transfer on death deed recorded before the owner's death, gives a buyer firmer footing.

Foreclosure timing also shows up in these records. A notice of sale must be posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk at least 21 days before the first-Tuesday auction, and Brazoria County charges $8.00 for a trustee notice.

The clerk adds a penalty fee. Texas Property Code 11.003 sets it at the greater of $25 or twice the statutory filing fee, charged on top of the regular recording cost.

Where Hays County keeps its records

The Hays County Clerk's Records Division is the county's keeper of official public records, an archive that runs back to 1848. It holds deeds, deeds of trust and liens. Search and buy copies through the clerk's online Self-Service portal, use the computers in the office lobby, or ask to read an archived record book at the counter. Questions about official records can go to recordsdivision@hayscountytx.gov.

Three divisions make up the clerk's office: Records, Courts and Commissioners Court. Courts handles probate and guardianship support, so start there if the homeowner has died. The District Clerk, a different office, holds divorce and family court files, and a decree that touches your title may mean a second stop.

San Marcos is the main location. Three substations also serve the public. All keep weekday hours of 8 am to 4:30 pm with a noon to 1 pm lunch break. Phone first to learn whether a substation will take your filing.

Searching land records online

The Self-Service portal opens with a disclaimer you must accept before you search. The clerk makes no certification of what the index displays, treats it as a rough catalogue, and urges you to try each spelling a name might take. Use the index to find the recorded document, then open the document itself and read it.

Four searches, run before listing, catch most nasty surprises:

  • Each owner on the chain of title, searched with and without middle initials, suffixes and former surnames.
  • Every deed of trust, followed by its matching release. A loan paid off years back can still look open when nobody filed the release.
  • Judgments, abstracts and state tax liens, which the Comptroller reports to the county clerk for entry in a separate lien book.
  • Notices of foreclosure sale, which the clerk posts and files.

A free service called Fraud Guard emails you whenever a document bearing your name is recorded. For a rental house or vacant lot, that is an inexpensive early warning against a forged deed.

What makes a deed recordable?

Texas law (Property Code 12.001(b)) bars a clerk from recording a deed until the signature has been acknowledged to a notary or similar officer, or sworn before two subscribing witnesses. Venue follows the parcel: whether the house is in Kyle, Wimberley or Dripping Springs, and wherever the seller now lives, the deed goes to Hays County.

Besides ordinary warranty deeds, the deed records take quitclaims, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds, affidavits, lien releases, leases, sale contracts and powers of attorney. The fee stacks up: $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for every page after, and then county add-ons for records management, archives and technology. If the grantee's mailing address is absent, expect $25 more. Request the exact total from the clerk prior to mailing.

Some buyers in federal or state grant programs can have recording fees waived if the commissioners court so directs its clerk. When your buyer is in such a program, ask whether Hays County has adopted a waiver.

Hays County housing at a glance

Hays County has grown fast since 2020. The mid-2025 estimate is 304,390 residents, a rise of 26.3% from the 2020 base, with 120,266 housing units. About 64.1% of homes are owner-occupied, and the middle value of those homes is $399,800. New subdivisions mean new plats, deeds of trust and liens, so a recently built house often carries more recorded paper than one that changed hands twice in thirty years.

Who values property and sends the tax bill?

Money matters belong to two other offices, not the clerk. Values, the property search and exemptions come from the Hays Central Appraisal District in Kyle. Bills and payments come from the Hays County Tax Office, because the district neither mails bills nor collects.

The district's office is 21001 North IH 35 in Kyle, phone (512) 268-2522, with a front-door drop box and weekday hours of 8 to 5. Its online forms cover a homestead exemption, an agricultural use application, a business personal property rendition and a change of address. Bills and payment instructions are at tax.co.hays.tx.us.

Each granted homestead gets an audit every five years (Tax Code 11.43(h-1)). Answer an audit letter promptly, enclosing a valid Texas driver's license or state ID with the house address on it, because silence puts a termination date on the exemption. Statewide, values are fixed January 1; homestead notices begin about April 1; protests are generally due by mid-May.

Record problems that slow a Hays County sale

Stale liens, tax arrears and absent heirs head the list. On January 1 each year a lien secures that year's tax, so whatever is unpaid stays attached through a sale. February 1 turns a bill still open after January 31 delinquent, adding a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest.

Inherited houses raise their own questions:

  • A transfer on death deed works only if recorded during the owner's life.
  • For a muniment of title, the court order and will go on file with the clerk.
  • An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement filed with the clerk, though a buyer or title company has no legal duty to rely on it.
  • Heirs whose names are not on a recorded deed must hand the appraisal district three things before claiming the homestead exemption: an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate and a current utility bill.

Foreclosure notices reach the clerk at least 21 days ahead of the first-Tuesday auction. Seeing one against a house means a countdown has begun.

Checklist before you list

Start by downloading the chain of title and noting each owner's name exactly as written. Pair every deed of trust with its release. Get a balance from the Hays County Tax Office for this year and earlier ones. Make sure the appraisal district has your homestead exemption and a correct mailing address. Where the owner has died, work out with a title company which route moves title to the buyer: probate, muniment of title or affidavit of heirship.

An as-is cash buyer still wants a clean transfer, so the title company records the new deed and any payoff releases with the clerk. Closing a gap in the records early protects the closing date.

On closing day, the title company pays off recorded loans, collects the tax due and sends the new deed to the clerk. Ask it for a list of what it found in the records so no item catches you by surprise at the table.

Frequently asked questions

Which office records a deed in Hays County?

The Records Division of the Hays County Clerk handles it, and its files reach back to 1848. A Hays County house is always filed with the Hays County Clerk.

Can I search Hays County deeds online?

Yes, through the clerk's Self-Service portal, where records can be viewed and purchased. You accept a disclaimer first, and the portal advises trying every spelling of a name.

Does the appraisal district record my deed?

No. The appraisal district sets value and handles exemptions from Kyle, while the clerk records the deed. Owners usually update the district separately, for example with its online change of address form.

Who sends the Hays County property tax bill?

The Hays County Tax Office mails the bills and accepts payment. Call it, not the appraisal district, with any question about an amount owed.

What happens if a deed has no grantee mailing address?

The clerk may add a $25 charge. List a mailing address for every buyer on the deed before you file.

Where Guadalupe County deed and lien records are kept

The County Clerk's Official Records Division in Seguin records deeds, mortgages, liens, plats and federal and state tax liens for Guadalupe County. The clerk is also the county recorder under the Texas Constitution, so a deed for any house in the county lands here regardless of where the owner lives. The county sits roughly one hundred miles inland from the Gulf of Mexico in south central Texas, part of the San Antonio metropolitan area.

Walk-in filers go to 211 West Court Street, Seguin, Texas 78155. A satellite office is at 1101 Elbel, Schertz, Texas 78154. Clerk staff cannot give legal advice or help draft wills, contracts or other legal instruments (Texas Government Code section 81.101), so have a deed prepared before you arrive. Call the Official Records Division before a trip to ask about hours and which services each counter offers.

The clerk's online Public Records Search lets anyone look up documents recorded under a name. Search your own name before listing the home to see each deed, lien and release attached to it, and show anything unfamiliar to a title company early.

Ways to file a deed

Deeds can be hand-delivered, mailed or submitted through an e-recording vendor. The clerk uses CSC, eRecording Partners Network (ePN), Simplifile, HopDox and ValueCheck for electronic filings.

The county sets its own formatting rules, and they are strict. Leave at least four inches at the foot of the document for the recording stamp. If the page does not have the space, an add-a-page goes on at no charge, and e-recording submitters can attach the clerk's Submitters Add-A-Page as the last sheet. Scans must be 600 dpi with a white background, black lettering and a font of at least 8 points, because the image becomes the permanent record.

  • To be recorded, a conveyance must be signed and then acknowledged before a notary or other authorized officer, or proved by two subscribing witnesses.
  • Deeds signed after December 31, 1981 need a mailing address for every grantee. Leave it out and the filer owes a penalty of $25 or double the recording fee, whichever is larger.
  • A properly prepared document must be recorded. The clerk has no power to turn one away because it might be fraudulent.

Recording charges

Base recording charges come from state law, as summarized in the county clerk manual that Texas courts publish for clerks. Page count, indexed names and added fees all change the total, so ask the clerk for the exact figure before mailing payment.

A commissioners court may order its clerk not to charge recording fees on real property for buyers in particular federal or state grant programs. If your buyer uses one, ask whether Guadalupe County has done so.

Getting a Guadalupe County deed ready to file

Before you head to Seguin or Schertz, check five things. The deed carries every signature, and the notary has completed the acknowledgment. Each grantee's mailing address is printed on it. There is at least four inches of blank space at the foot of the last page. The legal description matches the prior deed. You have a check or payment ready, since the exact total depends on pages and names.

If anything is wrong, the clerk cannot fix or draft it for you, so ask a title company or attorney. For a house with a mortgage, ask who files the release of lien after payoff. A cash buyer's closing usually adds just the deed and any lien releases to the clerk's queue.

Watching for deed fraud

Register for the clerk's free Recording Notification Service and an email arrives whenever a document is recorded under a name you watch. One registered email address can watch up to 10 names or variations, and the alert covers only Guadalupe County records filed after you sign up.

Scammers record fake deeds to pose as owners, then collect rent or sale money from victims. A recorded document stays permanent, and the only remedy is a court order, itself recorded, declaring it void. The clerk cannot take legal action for you. Owners who suspect fraud should contact the Guadalupe County Sheriff's Office at 830-303-4188 extension 1219, an attorney, the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov or the Texas Attorney General's consumer complaint page.

Vacant houses are the usual target. Check on empty property often, ask someone you trust to look in while you are away, let no mail pile up, and keep your mailing address current with the Guadalupe Appraisal District and the tax assessor-collector.

Records that come up when a house changes hands

A title search follows the chain of recorded instruments. Deeds of trust, releases, tax liens, foreclosure notices, probate orders and affidavits all end up in the clerk's files, and a missing link slows a closing.

  • Foreclosure auctions are preceded by a notice on the courthouse door and in the clerk's file, at least 21 days out.
  • The comptroller files notice of a state tax lien with the clerk, who enters it in the state tax lien book.
  • When a will is probated as a muniment of title, the order and will go to the clerk of the county where the land is.
  • A small estate affidavit that passes a homestead gets a recorded copy at the clerk's office.
  • A transfer on death deed has no effect unless it was recorded while the owner was alive.

Heirs sometimes discover that an old deed was never recorded. An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement on file, but no buyer or lender has to rely on it. When title is unclear, a court order holds up better.

The July 2025 estimate is 201,111 residents, a gain of 16.4 percent over the 172,729 on the April 2020 base. They share 77,249 housing units across 711.25 square miles, and the county issued 1,697 building permits in 2025, so new deeds and plats keep arriving at the clerk's counter. Homeowners occupy 77.8 percent of homes. The 2020 to 2024 middle home value is $304,400, and the middle rent is $1,517.

For tax questions the Guadalupe Appraisal District's number is 830.303.3313. The district values property at its January 1 status. It also describes deferrals that postpone tax without canceling it: a homestead deferral accrues 8 percent a year, and a deferral for owners 65 or older or disabled accrues 5 percent. Settle any deferral before closing on a sale.

Who records a deed for Guadalupe County land?

The County Clerk's Official Records Division at 211 West Court Street, Seguin, Texas 78155, or the Schertz satellite office at 1101 Elbel. Electronic filers go through CSC, ePN, Simplifile, HopDox or ValueCheck.

Does a document need a notary to be recorded?

In practice, yes. A conveyance needs a notary's or other authorized officer's acknowledgment, or proof before two subscribing witnesses. The clerk records qualifying documents in the order received.

How do I learn if a document was recorded against my property?

Look yourself up in the clerk's online records, then join the free Recording Notification Service. Each registered address can watch up to 10 names and gets an automated message on any new filing.

Can a fraudulent deed be removed?

No. A recorded document stays permanent, and only a court order recorded afterward shows that it is void. Contact the Sheriff's Office and an attorney quickly if you suspect fraud.

What does recording a deed cost?

Page one is $5.00 under state rules, each added page is $4.00, and each name past five is $0.25. Management, archive and technology fees go on top, so ask the clerk to quote the total.
